```{r}
fmt_pct <- function(x) vapply(x, function(v) {
  if (is.na(v)) return(NA_character_)
  if (v < 1e-4) return("<0.0001%")
  if (v < 1) { s <- formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 4)
    s <- sub("0+$", "", s); s <- sub("\\.$", "", s); return(paste0(s, "%")) }
  paste0(formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2), "%")
}, character(1))

## grouped, model-coloured, zebra-striped table (reproduces the old flextable look,
## but rendered natively inline instead of exported to .docx) --------------------
## Optional arguments (defaults leave every existing table unchanged):
##   col_colors : named character vector, value-column name -> body text colour.
##                Overrides the colour-by-group-name rule for the columns it names.
##   shade_cols : value-column names to tint (SHADE_BG, with a darker tint on the
##                zebra-striped rows so the striping stays visible).
SHADE_BG     <- "#e9f2ed"   # light tint of GREEN_HEADER
SHADE_BG_ALT <- "#dde9e2"   # same tint, zebra rows
style_grouped_table <- function(df, groups, subs, footer_text = NULL,
                                col_colors = NULL, shade_cols = NULL) {
  vcols  <- names(df)[-1]
  rle_g  <- rle(groups)
  top_w  <- c(1, rle_g$lengths)
  top_l  <- c("Scenario", rle_g$values)
  seps   <- c(1, head(1 + cumsum(rle_g$lengths), -1))          # right-edge group separators
  txtcol <- c(COL_MODEL_TXT, rolling = unname(COL_MODEL[["rolling"]]))
  bd     <- officer::fp_border(color = "#dddddd", width = 1)

  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- set_header_labels(ft, values = setNames(as.list(c("", subs)), c("Scenario", vcols)))
  ft <- add_header_row(ft, top = TRUE, values = top_l, colwidths = top_w)
  ft <- merge_at(ft, i = 1:2, j = 1, part = "header")
  ft <- bg(ft, part = "header", bg = GREEN_HEADER)
  ft <- color(ft, part = "header", color = "white")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- align(ft, align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "center", part = "header")
  ft <- bold(ft, j = 1, part = "body")
  for (g in unique(groups)) {
    gcols <- vcols[groups == g]
    col   <- if (tolower(g) %in% names(txtcol)) txtcol[[tolower(g)]] else NULL
    if (!is.null(col) && length(gcols)) ft <- color(ft, j = gcols, color = col, part = "body")
  }
  if (!is.null(col_colors))
    for (cc in intersect(names(col_colors), vcols))
      ft <- color(ft, j = cc, color = col_colors[[cc]], part = "body")
  ft <- bg(ft, i = seq(2, nrow(df), by = 2), bg = "#f5f5f2", part = "body")
  if (length(shade_cols)) {
    sc <- intersect(shade_cols, vcols)
    ft <- bg(ft, j = sc, bg = SHADE_BG, part = "body")
    ft <- bg(ft, i = seq(2, nrow(df), by = 2), j = sc, bg = SHADE_BG_ALT, part = "body")
  }
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline(ft, i = 1, part = "header", border = officer::fp_border(color = "white", width = 1))
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "header")
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "body")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding.top = 4, padding.bottom = 4, part = "all")
  ## Give every value column the SAME width so the left/right model groups stay
  ## symmetric. Widths are measured BEFORE the footer is added, so a long
  ## footnote wraps instead of widening the columns.
  wv <- dim_pretty(ft)$widths
    wv <- dim_pretty(ft)$widths
  w  <- c(wv[1], rep(max(wv[-1]), length(vcols)))    # Scenario natural; value columns equal
  w  <- w * min(1, TABLE_MAX_W / sum(w))             # shrink to fit the page if too wide
  ft <- width(ft, j = seq_len(ncol(df)), width = w)
  if (!is.null(footer_text)) {
    ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
    ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 8.5, part = "footer")
    ft <- color(ft, color = "grey40", part = "footer")
  }
  set_table_properties(ft, layout = "fixed")
}
```

# Project Overview

This project asks whether accounting for non-stationarity leads to
better land-acquisition decisions for waterfowl conservation in the U.S.
Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) under different climate scenarios. It
builds three decision models and compares their performance across
climate-change scenarios and a stationary null.

The three models acquire land period by period (decadal steps,
2020–2100) under a budget constraint:

- **Greedy** — status-quo heuristic: rank parcels by current
  benefit-to-cost ratio, buy down the list. No foresight.
- **Myopic ILP** — re-optimizes each decade but freezes current benefit
  and hazard and assumes they persist (a fabricated stationary future);
  implements the current decade, then re-solves.
- **Rolling-horizon ILP** — same structure, but uses the true projected
  trajectories. The foresighted benchmark. Uses Gurobi solver (academic
  license).

The spatial unit is the **EAU** (Equal Area Unit, \~342 km²). After
dropping 4 Wetland Management Districts, the analysis uses **879 EAUs
across 20 WMDs**, over **9 decadal periods** and **5 scenarios** (RCP
4.5/8.5 × wet/dry, plus a stationary null).

# Data Sources

- **Benefit**: McKenna, Owen P., et al. "Conservation enhances
  resilience of the United States Duck Factory as environmental shifts
  may diminish landscape-scale waterfowl breeding capacity." BioScience
  (2026): biag091.
  - projects breeding duck pairs over RCP 4.5/8.5 × wet/dry scenarios.
  - linear interpolation to get from obs/mid-century/end of century to
    decadal time steps.
- **Cost**: Nolte, Christoph. "High-resolution land value maps reveal
  underestimation of conservation costs in the United States.".
  Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 117.47 (2020):
  29577-29583.
  - assume 2% unfiform annual increase
  - note no emissions or precip scenarios.
- **Risk**: FOREsce (derived). Sohl, Terry L., et al. "Spatially
  explicit land-use and land-cover scenarios for the Great Plains of the
  United States." Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 153 (2012):
  1-15.
  - `r lc_label`
  - calculated as gross suitable habitat loss per time step.
  - note this has RCP 4.5 & 8.5 scenarios, but no precip scenario.

# Model Formulation

**Decision model.** EAUs are indexed over $i \in \mathcal{I}$ and $t \in \{0, \dots, T\}$ index decades (0 =
2020, $T = 8$ = 2100). For EAU $i$ in period $t$, $b_{i,t}$ is the
projected breeding duck pairs under a given scenario; $\lambda_{i,t}$ is
the per-period probability that its suitable habitat is converted; and
$c_{i,t}$ is the cost of acquisition (land value per hectare × EAU area,
inflated at 2% per year).

*Survival.* If EAU $i$ is not acquired, the probability that it remains
unconverted through period $t$ is

$$S_{i,0} = 1, \qquad S_{i,t} = \prod_{s=0}^{t-1} \left(1 - \lambda_{i,s}\right), \quad t \ge 1.$$

where for a given EAU, its per-decade survival probability is defined as 1-$\lambda_{i,t}$ and the cumulative survival probability in time $t$ is the product of each decade's survival probability from 2020 through the decade just before $t$ ($t$-1). 

*Acquisition value.* The conservation value of acquiring an EAU is calculated as the expected loss its acquisition prevents. Acquiring EAU $i$ in period $\tau$ protects its benefit with certainty from $\tau$ onward.

$$V_{i,\tau} = \sum_{t=\tau}^{T} \delta^{t}\, b_{i,t} \left(1 - S_{i,t}\right),$$
where $V_{i,\tau}$ is the value of acquiring parcel $i$ in period
$\tau$, expressed as the total time-discounted sum of duck-pairs from $\tau$ through 2100; $\delta$ is the decadal
discount factor (0.95); $b_{i,t}$ is the projected benefit (duck
pairs) in parcel $i$ in period $t$ under a given scenario; and
$S_{i,t}$ is the probability that parcel $i$ survives (i.e., remains
unconverted) through period $t$ if it is not acquired, so that
$1 - S_{i,t}$ is the probability of conversion. Total landscape value under any acquisition schedule equals the
value of doing nothing plus $\sum_i V_{i,\tau_i}$ (i.e., the sum of acquisition value), summed over all acquired parcel.

All unacquired parcels are treated as
available (i.e. subject to conversion risk) at each re-solve;
conversion does not remove parcels from the set, but instead enters
**only** through the weighting in the objective. Acquisition removes
this weight and counts the full (time-discounted) value; unacquired
parcels retain only their survival-discounted value.

*Greedy policy.* The greedy policy does not solve an optimization problem.
At each decision period $\tau$, it ranks every available EAU
$i \in \mathcal{A}_\tau$ by its current benefit-to-cost ratio,

$$r_{i,\tau} = \frac{b_{i,\tau}}{c_{i,\tau}},$$

the number of duck pairs per dollar today. It then works down the list from
highest to lowest ratio. It buys each EAU whose cost fits within the budget
remaining in period $\tau$ and skips any that doesn't fit. It stops when it
reaches the end of the list. The greedy policy ignores conversion risk, since $\lambda$
never enters the ranking. It ignores the future, because it considers only
period $\tau$ and plans no later purchases. And it doesn't search for the best
combination within the period: ranking by ratio can leave a better-value set
of parcels unpurchased. Greedy represents a common status-quo approach to
prioritizing acquisitions: buy the most habitat per dollar available now.


*Optimization.* The rolling and myopic policies use an ILP approach, employing a Gurobi solver. If EAU $i$ is acquired in period $t$, then $x_{i,t} \in \{0,1\}$ equals 1;  $\mathcal{A}_\tau$ is the set of EAUs not yet acquired at the start of period $\tau$. At each decision period $\tau$, the ILP policies solves to maximize V (acquisition value) according to:

$$\max_{x} \; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}_\tau} \sum_{t=\tau}^{T} \hat{V}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}$$
where $\hat{V}$ is the belief about expected value (i.e., discounted duck pairs saved). The ILP policies differ only in $\hat{V}$. For the rolling-horizon policy, $\hat{V}_{i,t} = V_{i,t}$, computed from the projected trajectories of
$b$ and $\lambda$. For the myopic policy, benefit and hazard are held at their period-$\tau$ values for the whole horizon, so the coefficients are recomputed at every solve.

In both policies, maximization of expected benefit is subject to:

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t=\tau}^{T} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall\, i \in \mathcal{A}_\tau && \text{(each EAU acquired at most once)} \\
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}_\tau} c_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_t && \forall\, t = \tau, \dots, T && \text{(per-period budget)} \\
x_{i,t} &\in \{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}$$

Only the period-$\tau$ decisions are carried out. Then
$\mathcal{A}_{\tau+1}$ (the current set of available parcels) is re-evaluated
and the problem is solved again. Conversion does not remove parcels from
$\mathcal{A}_\tau$; it enters only through the weight $(1 - S_{i,t})$.


*Budget.* The budget for each period is

$$B_t = k \cdot \operatorname*{median}_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \left(c_{i,t}\right), \qquad k = 5 \;\; (\text{sensitivity: } k \in \{2, 10\}).$$

Because all costs inflate at the same rate, $B_t$ is constant in real
terms. The budget cannot be carried forward or borrowed against. The
greedy policy is held to the same $B_t$: in each period it acquires
available EAUs in decreasing order of $b_{i,t}/c_{i,t}$ until no
remaining EAU fits within what is left of $B_t$.

# Results

## Descriptive Summary

### Duck distribution

Consistent with other studies (e.g., McKenna et al, 2026), duck
abundance is higher in the western portion of the PPR than the eastern
portion. This overall distribution pattern continues through 2100 (Fig.
1). In all scenarios, duck abundance is predicted to decline across the
PPR by 2100, although wet scenarios fare better than dry scenarios (Fig.
2). Note that this figure was produced after a spatial join error was
corrected.

```{r}
#| label: fig-benefit-map
#| fig-cap: !expr caps$fig_benefit_map
#| out-width: 100%
#| eval: !expr desc_maps_ok
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT_DIR, "map_benefit_2020_2100.png"))
```


{{< pagebreak >}}

### Risk

Risk of conversion across all EAUs is heavily skewed, with the vast
majority of EAUs showing a nearly zero per period conversion risk; the
maximum per period conversion risk for a given EAU is \~15%. There is a
sharp drop in per period conversion risk in 2050, which is a function of
the FOREsce model: cropland conversion is frontloaded through 2050, at
which point conversions to cropland decline. Note that this metric has
been corrected from net habitat loss to gross habitat loss.

```{r}
#| label: fig-risk-box
#| fig-cap: !expr caps$fig_risk_box
#| out-width: 100%
#| eval: !expr desc_ok
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT_DIR, "fig_risk_box.png"))
```

## Model results

## Relative performance of acquisition policies

The major findings of this study compare the difference between total
benefit secured across the landscape (2020-2100) under the rolling ILP
policy as compared to the greedy or myopic policy. As expected, the
rolling policy outperforms both the myopic and the greedy policy; the
performance gap between the rolling policy and the greedy policy is
larger than the rolling-myopic gap. Rolling provides a 18-20%
improvement over myopic, and a \~49-57% improvement over greedy. Under
stationarity, there is virtually no difference (as expected, since a
stationary environment provides no penalty for policies without
foresight). The rolling policy outperforms the myopic and greedy
policies under all climate scenarios, consistent with our expectations
that an acquisition policy with foresight should outperform a policy
with no or limited foresight under any degree of non-stationarity.

**My interpretation: A non-stationary, climate-aware acquisition policy
could deliver a \~50% improvement in conservation outcomes as compared
to the greedy (i.e., status quo) acquisition policy in use today,
potentially protecting an additional 37,000-69,000 of cumulative duck pairs by 2100**.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gap-vs-rolling
#| tbl-cap: !expr caps$tbl_gap_vs_rolling
style_grouped_table(
  tbl1, groups1, subs1,
  col_colors = cols1, shade_cols = shade1,
  footer_text = c(
    "Acquisition Value = cumulative discounted duck-pairs secured relative to the do-nothing baseline, 2020\u20132100.",
    paste0(DP, " = pairs secured through acquisition under rolling \u2212 greedy (or myopic)."),
        "% improvement = \u0394pairs as % of greedy (or myopic).",
    if (any(abs(c(t1$rg_dpairs, t1$rm_dpairs)) < 1))
      "\u2014 = difference of <1 pair; % improvement not meaningful at this scale."))
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

Another way of describing this is to ask how short of optimal the greedy
and myopic policies fall. Here, the rolling policy is used as the
provably near-optimal benchmark (MIP gap 0.01% across all rolling
solves), and performance gaps are expressed as a % of rolling. The
myopic policy falls \~15-17% short of rolling, and the greedy policy
falls \~33-36% short of rolling.

**My interpretation: Current use of acquisition policies that assume
environmental stationarity fall short of an optimal acquisition policy
by \~30%, failing to secure an additional 37,000-69,000 potential cumulative duck
pairs by 2100**.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shortfall-vs-rolling
#| tbl-cap: !expr caps$tbl_shortfall_vs_rolling
style_grouped_table(
  tbl1s, groups1s, subs1s,
  col_colors = cols1, shade_cols = shade1,
  footer_text = c(
    "Acquisition Value = cumulative discounted duck-pairs secured relative to the do-nothing baseline, 2020\u20132100.",
    paste0(DP, " = secured through acquisition under rolling \u2212 greedy (or myopic)."),
    "% shortfall = \u0394pairs, as % of rolling.",
    if (any(abs(c(t1$rg_dpairs, t1$rm_dpairs)) < 1))
      "\u2014 = difference of <1 pair; % shortfall not meaningful at this scale."))
```

## Relative performance over time

This graph shows how the gap between the rolling policy and the
myopic/greedy policies grows over time. This is presented as net changes
in duck pairs, using the rolling policy as a benchmark (value added gap
for rolling = 0). As expected, the cumulative gap in performance between
rolling and greedy/myopic grows over time (negative values only); and
greedy is substantially worse than myopic (red always \< yellow).

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Acquisition value over baseline

This table compares the total benefit secured across the landscape
(2020-2100) through the three acquisition policies against a
"do-nothing" baseline scenario in which no parcels are acquired. All
acquisition policies outperform the do-nothing baseline under climate
change scenarios; there is no improvement under assumptions of
stationarity (as expected: stationarity freezes conversion risk to
effectively zero).

Even a greedy acquisition policy outperforms a do-nothing policy; myopic
and rolling policies each respectively improve upon that baseline. As
expected based on the duck density projections, wet/dry scenario is a
larger determinant of improvement than RCP scenario.

Overall improvement of any acquisition policy, expressed in % over
baseline, is relatively small (0.64% at best). This is likely an
artifact of how conversion risk is being calculated in this model (a
measure of habitat erosion standing in for habitat conversion
probability). It may also be related to a relatively conservative budget
parameter (only \~60-70 EAUs are acquired in most scenarios). That said,
these numbers might not be that different from real world estimates:
Kemink et al 2023 estimated that the program impact for SWAP was "an
avoided loss between 0.00% and 0.02% of the carrying capacity for broods
and breeding waterfowl from 2008–2017."

Interpretation here is that light blue parcels are where the rolling

### 10/26/2026: Conversion risk sensitivity analysis

```{r}
#| label: hsw-setup
#| include: false
## Assets are written by the hazard-sweep section of 10_results_assets.R from the canonical run
## (k = 1) and every complete high-hazard run made by 15_run_hazard_sweep.R.
swmeta <- tryCatch(
  jsonlite::read_json(file.path(OUT_DIR, "haz_sweep_metadata.json"), simplifyVector = TRUE),
  error = function(e) NULL)
sw_ok     <- !is.null(swmeta) && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "haz_sweep.csv"))
sw_fig_ok <- function(f) sw_ok && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, f))
sw_stale  <- sw_ok && isTRUE(swmeta$any_stale)

sw <- if (sw_ok) read_csv(file.path(OUT_DIR, "haz_sweep.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL
CLIM_SW <- c("rcp45_wet", "rcp45_dry", "rcp85_wet", "rcp85_dry")
CANON_DISPLAY <- "FOREsce derived"   # shown in place of script 10's "Canonical" label

## numbers used inline in the prose
sw_n      <- if (sw_ok) nrow(swmeta$runs) else 0
sw_canon  <- if (sw_ok) sprintf("%.2f%%", swmeta$canonical_annual_pct) else "?"
sw_max    <- if (sw_ok) sprintf("%.2f%%", max(swmeta$runs$annual_rate_pct)) else "?"
sw_kmax   <- if (sw_ok) sprintf("%.1f", max(swmeta$runs$k)) else "?"

## "min–max" across the four climate scenarios
fmt_rng <- function(lo, hi) ifelse(is.na(lo), "\u2014",
  ifelse(abs(hi - lo) < 0.05, sprintf("%.1f%%", lo), sprintf("%.1f\u2013%.1f%%", lo, hi)))

## Same table look as the land-cover comparison tables.
style_sweep_table <- function(df, groups, subs, footer_text = NULL,
                              first_lab = "Annual rate", font_size = 8.5) {
  rle_g <- rle(groups)
  seps  <- c(1, head(1 + cumsum(rle_g$lengths), -1))
  bd    <- officer::fp_border(color = "#dddddd", width = 1)
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- set_header_labels(ft, values = setNames(as.list(c("", subs)), names(df)))
  ft <- add_header_row(ft, top = TRUE, values = c(first_lab, rle_g$values),
                       colwidths = c(1, rle_g$lengths))
  ft <- merge_at(ft, i = 1:2, j = 1, part = "header")
  ft <- bg(ft, part = "header", bg = GREEN_HEADER)
  ft <- color(ft, part = "header", color = "white")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- align(ft, align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1:2, align = "left", part = "all")
  ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "center", part = "header")
  ft <- bold(ft, j = 1, part = "body")
  if (nrow(df) > 1) ft <- bg(ft, i = seq(2, nrow(df), by = 2), bg = "#f5f5f2", part = "body")
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline(ft, i = 1, part = "header", border = officer::fp_border(color = "white", width = 1))
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "header")
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "body")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding.top = 3, padding.bottom = 3, padding.left = 3,
                padding.right = 3, part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = font_size, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)                      # header + body only: footer not added yet
   wv <- dim(ft)$widths                                         # per-column widths (in)
  ft <- width(ft, width = wv * min(1, TABLE_MAX_W / sum(wv)))  # shrink to fit the page
  if (!is.null(footer_text)) {
    ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
    ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 7.5, part = "footer")
    ft <- color(ft, color = "grey40", part = "footer")
    ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")
  }
  set_table_properties(ft, layout = "fixed")
}

## captions (edit here) ----------------------------------------------------------

                       "across conversion rates. Range across the four climate scenarios.")
cap_sw_pct   <- paste0("**Policy performance across conversion rates (% improvement).** ",
                       "Left: myopic vs. greedy (value of using conversion risk); middle: rolling ",
                       "vs. myopic (value of foresight); right: rolling vs. greedy (total). ",
                       "Each tick gives the annual rate and the estimate it stands for.")
cap_sw_pairs <- paste0("Policy performance across conversion rates (", "$\\Delta$",
                       "pairs). Same comparisons as the previous figure, in discounted ",
                       "duck-pairs rather than percent.")
cap_sw_risk  <- paste0("**Per-period conversion risk across EAUs, by decade and emissions scenario.** ",
                       "Colour = annual conversion rate of each run (", CANON_DISPLAY, " = lightest). ",
                       "Box = median and IQR; diamond = mean; dash = maximum.")
```

```{r}
    "Rerun 15_run_hazard_sweep.R and 10_results_assets.R before relying",
    "on this section.)*")
```

In an effort to compare our model results to published estimates of landscape-scale conversion rates for wetlands and grasslands, I re-ran the model with conversion risk rescaled to different conversion rates. The FORESce derived conversion risk data acts as a lower bound: the landscape average of suitable-to-unsuitable habitat transition is equivalent to a 0.17% annual rate in 2020. Other published estimates vary, ranging from 0.28% (Johnston et al 2013) to 1.33% (Rashford et al. 2011).

I re-scaled all conversion risk values so that the mean landscape-wide 2020 conversion rate (i.e., the share of all unprotected suitable habitat converted per decade) equaled the target rate. I calculated a scaling factor, k, which would bring the mean landscape-scale conversion rate to the literature-derived rate, then applied that scaling factor to the conversion risk table in every EAU in every decade. This approach multiplies the underlying conversion rate by the same factor in every EAU, decade and scenario, so the spatial pattern and the trajectory of conversion risk over time (including the mid-century collapse under GCAM) are unchanged. Benefit, cost, budget and land cover are identical to the original run.

We find that the overall pattern of rolling outperforms myopic which outperforms greedy still holds. The performance gap, however, narrows. Rather than ~50% improvement of rolling > greedy, for example, we see ~ 35-40% improvement. The value of the rolling policy as compared to the myopic or greedy policy declines as conversion risk rises.

```{r}
  summarise(rm_lo = min(rm_pct), rm_hi = max(rm_pct),
            rg_lo = min(rg_pct), rg_hi = max(rg_pct),
            ranking = all(ranking_holds), .groups = "drop") %>%

df <- data.frame(Rate  = sprintf("%.2f%%", tb$annual_rate_pct),
                 Bench = ifelse(tb$label == "Canonical", CANON_DISPLAY, tb$label),
                 K     = sprintf("%.2f", tb$k),

                 rg    = fmt_rng(tb$rg_lo, tb$rg_hi),
                 ord   = ifelse(tb$ranking, "Yes", "NO"), check.names = FALSE)
style_sweep_table(df,
  groups = c("Run", "Run", "Rolling vs. Myopic", "Rolling vs. Greedy", "Ranking holds"),
  subs   = c("Benchmark", "k", "", "", "all scenarios"),
  footer_text = c("% improvement = (better policy \u2212 comparison policy) as % of the comparison policy's value; range across the four climate scenarios.",
                  "Annual rate = target rate per year; for the canonical run, its habitat-weighted 2020 rate."))
```

**Data Sources:**
Johnston et al 2013: Johnston, Carol A. "Wetland losses due to row crop expansion in the Dakota Prairie Pothole Region." Wetlands 33.1 (2013): 175-182. 0.28% annual NWI wetland loss rate. 

Stephens et al 20028: Stephens, Scott E., et al. "Predicting risk of habitat conversion in native temperate grasslands." Conservation biology 22.5 (2008): 1320-1330. 0.4% annualized probability of conversion from grassland to cropland, 1989-2003

Kemink et al 2023: Kemink, Kaylan M., et al. "Assessing prioritization measures for a private land conservation program in the US Prairie Pothole Region." Conservation Science and Practice 5.7 (2023): e12939. 0.57% estimated upper bound for wetland drainage rates. 

Rashford et al 2011: Rashford, Benjamin S., Johann A. Walker, and Christopher T. Bastian. "Economics of grassland conversion to cropland in the Prairie Pothole Region." Conservation Biology 25.2 (2011): 276-284.

### 10/21/2026: Budget sensitivity analysis

```{r}
#| label: bud-setup
#| include: false
## Budget-sweep assets are written by the budget section of 10_results_assets.R into the canonical
## run's output_figs (bud_* files), from the runs made by 13_run_budget_sweep.R.
bmeta <- tryCatch(
  jsonlite::read_json(file.path(OUT_DIR, "bud_metadata.json"), simplifyVector = TRUE),
  error = function(e) NULL)
bud_ok      <- !is.null(bmeta) &&
               file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "bud_headline.csv")) &&
               file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "bud_value_added.csv"))
bud_conv_ok <- bud_ok && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "bud_convergence.csv"))
bud_fig_ok  <- function(f) bud_ok && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, f))

BUDS      <- if (bud_ok) bmeta$budgets else numeric(0)
B_CANON   <- if (bud_ok) bmeta$canonical_budget else 5
EAU_HA    <- if (bud_ok) bmeta$eau_area_ha else NA_real_
bud_list  <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) format(x) else
  paste0(paste(format(x[-length(x)]), collapse = ", "), " and ", format(x[length(x)]))

## sentence on the canonical-budget rerun (inline in the prose below)
canon_sentence <- if (bud_ok && !is.null(bmeta$canon_check)) {
  cc <- bmeta$canon_check
  if (isTRUE(cc$identical))
    paste0("The rerun at the canonical budget (", B_CANON, " EAUs per period) reproduced ",
           "the main results exactly.")
  else
    paste0("The rerun at the canonical budget (", B_CANON, " EAUs per period) matched the ",
           "main results to within ", signif(cc$max_abs_diff_pct, 2),
           "% of acquisition value.")
} else ""

## budget label in tables
bud_cell <- function(b) format(b)
FOOT_CANON <- paste0("* = canonical budget (", B_CANON,
                     " median-priced EAUs per period), as in the main results above.")

## Table style: the house look of style_grouped_table in 11_results.qmd, with any
## number of leading label columns (here Scenario + Budget). The first label column
## is merged down each scenario block, and blocks (not rows) are zebra-striped.
style_bud_table <- function(df, n_lead, lead_labs, groups, subs, footer_text = NULL,
                            col_colors = NULL, font_size = 8.5) {
  vcols <- names(df)[-(seq_len(n_lead))]
  rle_g <- rle(groups)
  seps  <- c(n_lead, head(n_lead + cumsum(rle_g$lengths), -1))
  bd    <- officer::fp_border(color = "#dddddd", width = 1)
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- set_header_labels(ft, values = setNames(as.list(c(rep("", n_lead), subs)), names(df)))
  ft <- add_header_row(ft, top = TRUE, values = c(lead_labs, rle_g$values),
                       colwidths = c(rep(1, n_lead), rle_g$lengths))
  for (j in seq_len(n_lead)) ft <- merge_at(ft, i = 1:2, j = j, part = "header")
  ft <- bg(ft, part = "header", bg = GREEN_HEADER)
  ft <- color(ft, part = "header", color = "white")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- align(ft, align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  ft <- valign(ft, j = seq_len(n_lead), valign = "center", part = "header")
  ft <- bold(ft, j = 1, part = "body")
  if (!is.null(col_colors))
    for (cc in intersect(names(col_colors), vcols))
      ft <- color(ft, j = cc, color = col_colors[[cc]], part = "body")
  ## zebra by block of the first label column, and a thin rule between blocks
  blk  <- cumsum(c(TRUE, df[[1]][-1] != df[[1]][-nrow(df)]))
  even <- which(blk %% 2 == 0)
  if (length(even)) ft <- bg(ft, i = even, bg = "#f5f5f2", part = "body")
  ends <- which(diff(blk) != 0)
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  if (length(ends)) ft <- hline(ft, i = ends, border = bd, part = "body")
  ft <- merge_v(ft, j = 1)
  ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top", part = "body")
  ft <- hline(ft, i = 1, part = "header", border = officer::fp_border(color = "white", width = 1))
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "header")
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "body")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding.top = 2, padding.bottom = 2, padding.left = 3,
                padding.right = 3, part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = font_size, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)                      # header + body only: footer not added yet
   wv <- dim(ft)$widths                                         # per-column widths (in)
  ft <- width(ft, width = wv * min(1, TABLE_MAX_W / sum(wv)))  # shrink to fit the page
  if (!is.null(footer_text)) {
    ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
    ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 7.5, part = "footer")
    ft <- color(ft, color = "grey40", part = "footer")
    ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")
  }
  set_table_properties(ft, layout = "fixed")
}

## body text coloured by the policy each column refers to (as in the main tables)
TXT_G <- COL_MODEL_TXT[["greedy"]]; TXT_M <- COL_MODEL_TXT[["myopic"]]
TXT_R <- COL_MODEL[["rolling"]]

## data ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    pivot_wider(names_from = model,
                values_from = c(value_added, pct_over_baseline, n_acquired, hectares)) %>%
    arrange(scenario, budget)
  ranking_all <- all(bh$ranking_holds[bh$scenario != "stationary"])
}
lead_cols <- function(d) data.frame(Scenario = unname(SCEN_LAB1[as.character(d$scenario)]),
                                    Budget   = bud_cell(d$budget), check.names = FALSE)
pct_or_dash <- function(dp, p) ifelse(abs(dp) < 1 | is.na(p), "\u2014", fmt_pct(p))

## captions (edit here) -------------------------------------------------------------
bud_caps <- list(
  fig_improvement = paste(
    "**Improvement of the rolling policy over greedy and myopic policies, by budget.**",
    "% improvement = (rolling \u2212 comparison policy) as % of the comparison policy's",

  tbl_improvement =
    "**Improvement of the rolling policy over greedy and myopic policies, by budget and scenario.**",
  tbl_shortfall =
    "**Shortfall of greedy and myopic policies relative to the rolling policy, by budget and scenario.**",
  fig_overtime = paste(
    "**Cumulative performance relative to the rolling policy, by budget.** Discounted",
    "duck-pairs secured by the greedy and myopic policies minus those secured by rolling,",
    "cumulative to 2100. Rows = climate scenario; columns = budget (median-priced EAUs",
    "per period). Rolling is the benchmark (0)."),
  fig_value = paste(
    "**Acquisition value by budget and policy.** Cumulative discounted duck-pairs secured",
    "relative to the do-nothing baseline, 2020\u20132100, by climate scenario."),
  tbl_over_baseline =
    "**Value of acquisition policy over do-nothing baseline, by budget and scenario.**",
  tbl_acquired =
    "**EAUs acquired by 2100, by policy, budget and scenario.**",
  fig_foresight = paste(
    "**Rolling vs. myopic acquisition sets, by budget.** EAUs colored by which policy buys",
    "them. Rows = climate scenario; columns = budget (median-priced EAUs per period).",
    "Purple cells are acquired under both policies; blue cells only under the rolling",
    "policy; orange cells are bought by the myopic policy but avoided by the rolling policy."),
  tbl_convergence =
    "**Solver convergence by budget and policy (all scenarios).**"
)
```


We wanted to explore the role of budget in determining the relatively performance of the three acquisition policies, as well as the overall performance over the do-nothing baseline. I re-ran the model with a stricter budget constraint (2 median-priced EAUs acquired per period) and a more generous budget constraint (10 median-priced EAUs per period) under all climate scenarios, using the GCAM reference landcover scenario. 

I found that across climate scenarios, a stricter budget constraint increased the performance gap between acquisition policies. When only 2 median-priced EAUs can be purchased per decision period, the rolling policy outperforms greedy/myopic policy by ~ 75%/25%; when 10 median-priced EAUs can be purchased per decision period, the rolling policy outperforms the greedy/myopic policy by only ~ 35%/~15%.

**The value of foresight increases under a stricter budget, and declines under a more generous budget**.

### 10/21/2026: Land-cover scenario comparison (GCAM reference vs. BAU)

```{r}
#| label: cmp-setup
#| include: false
## Comparison assets are written by the land-cover section of 10_results_assets.R from this run
## (base) and the run named by its COMPARE_RUN. Differences are alternative − base.
cmeta <- tryCatch(
  jsonlite::read_json(file.path(OUT_DIR, "cmp_metadata.json"), simplifyVector = TRUE),
  error = function(e) NULL)
cmp_ok      <- !is.null(cmeta) && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "cmp_value_added.csv"))
cmp_risk_ok <- cmp_ok && file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "cmp_risk_table.csv")) &&
               file.exists(file.path(OUT_DIR, "fig_cmp_risk_box.png"))
SB <- if (cmp_ok) cmeta$base_short else "base"
SA <- if (cmp_ok) cmeta$alt_short  else "alternative"
TH <- if (cmp_ok) cmeta$thresh_pp  else 2

fmt_p1  <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "\u2014", sprintf("%.1f%%", x))
fmt_pp1 <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "\u2014", sprintf("%+.1f", x))
fmt_rk  <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "\u2014", ifelse(x < 0.01, sprintf("%.3f%%", x), sprintf("%.2f%%", x)))

## Table style for the comparison tables: the same look and the same "autofit" layout
## as style_grouped_table in 11_results.qmd. Columns are sized to their header and
## body text (autofit runs BEFORE the footer is added, so a long footnote cannot
## widen a column), and tables with many columns use a smaller font so they fit
## the page. Footnotes are kept short: in the PDF they do not wrap.
style_cmp_table <- function(df, groups, subs, footer_text = NULL, bold_cells = NULL,
                            first_lab = "Scenario", font_size = 8.5) {
  rle_g <- rle(groups)
  seps  <- c(1, head(1 + cumsum(rle_g$lengths), -1))
  bd    <- officer::fp_border(color = "#dddddd", width = 1)
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- set_header_labels(ft, values = setNames(as.list(c("", subs)), names(df)))
  ft <- add_header_row(ft, top = TRUE, values = c(first_lab, rle_g$values),
                       colwidths = c(1, rle_g$lengths))
  ft <- merge_at(ft, i = 1:2, j = 1, part = "header")
  ft <- bg(ft, part = "header", bg = GREEN_HEADER)
  ft <- color(ft, part = "header", color = "white")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- align(ft, align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "center", part = "header")
  ft <- bold(ft, j = 1, part = "body")
  if (nrow(df) > 1) ft <- bg(ft, i = seq(2, nrow(df), by = 2), bg = "#f5f5f2", part = "body")
  for (bc in bold_cells) ft <- bold(ft,  i = bc[1], j = bc[2], part = "body")
  for (bc in bold_cells) ft <- color(ft, i = bc[1], j = bc[2], color = "#B0413E", part = "body")
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline(ft, i = 1, part = "header", border = officer::fp_border(color = "white", width = 1))
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "header")
  ft <- vline(ft, j = seps, border = bd, part = "body")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding.top = 3, padding.bottom = 3, padding.left = 3,
                padding.right = 3, part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = font_size, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)                      # header + body only: footer not added yet
   wv <- dim(ft)$widths                                         # per-column widths (in)
  ft <- width(ft, width = wv * min(1, TABLE_MAX_W / sum(wv)))  # shrink to fit the page
  if (!is.null(footer_text)) {
    ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
    ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 7.5, part = "footer")
    ft <- color(ft, color = "grey40", part = "footer")
    ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")
  }
  set_table_properties(ft, layout = "fixed")
}

## captions (edit here) ----------------------------------------------------------
cap_cmp_headline <- paste0("Improvement of the rolling policy over greedy/myopic, ",
                           SB, " vs. ", SA, " land cover.")
cap_cmp_value    <- paste0("Acquisition value (cumulative discounted duck-pairs secured relative to the do-nothing baseline, ",
                           "2020\u20132100), by policy and land-cover run. Note the absolute improvement of any acquisition policy, relative to do-nothing, in BAU vs GCAM.")
cap_cmp_risk_fig <- paste0("**Per-period conversion risk across EAUs, by decade, emissions scenario and land-cover scenario. Note that conversion risk collapses mid-century in GCAM, but stays constant in BAU.** Grey = ",
                           SB, "; red = ", SA, ". Box = median and IQR; diamond = mean; dash = maximum.")
cap_cmp_risk_tbl <- paste0("**Per-period conversion risk across EAUs, by decade and emissions scenario** (",
                           SB, " vs. ", SA, ").")
```


In order to explore the role of landcover trends and patterns on model results, I re-ran the model with another FOREsce projection (BAU). Both BAU and GCAM reference are considered to be likely scenarios in a world with no major agricultural or climate policy changes (as per the FORESce description):

- BAU: "Based on an extrapolation of recent land-cover trends as derived from remote-sensing data. Overall trends were provided by 2001 to 2011 change in the National Land Cover Database, while change in crop types were extrapolated from 2008 to 2014 change in the Cropland Data Layer. Overall the scenario is marked by expansion of high-value traditional crops (corn, soybeans, cotton), with a concurrent decline in dryland wheat and some other lower-value crops."

- GCAM: "Based on global-scale scenarios from the GCAM model, the "reference" scenario provides a likely landscape under a world without specific carbon or climate mitigation efforts. As such, it's another form of a "business-as-usual" scenario."

I wanted to compare these to see how changes in landcover estimations might affect model results, and specifically to see if the BAU scenario contained higher conversion rates than the GCAM scenario; it was noticeable in the GCAM scenario that conversion rates declined markedly mid-century, and wanted to explore what effect that would have.

I found that the policy ranking (rolling outperforms myopic which outperforms greedy) holds in both land-cover scenarios under both landcover projections. While the ranking holds, the magnitude of the performance gap varies between the landcover scenarios: the rolling policy still outperforms greedy and myopic in the BAU, but by substantially less than under the GCAM scenario.

{{< pagebreak >}}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cmp-headline
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_cmp_headline
#| eval: !expr cmp_ok
hd <- read_csv(file.path(OUT_DIR, "cmp_headline.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
df <- data.frame(Scenario = unname(SCEN_LAB1[hd$scenario]),
                 rg_b = fmt_p1(hd$rg_pct_base), rg_a = fmt_p1(hd$rg_pct_alt), rg_d = fmt_pp1(hd$rg_pct_diff),
                 rm_b = fmt_p1(hd$rm_pct_base), rm_a = fmt_p1(hd$rm_pct_alt), rm_d = fmt_pp1(hd$rm_pct_diff),
                 ord  = ifelse(hd$ranking_holds, "Yes", "NO"), check.names = FALSE)
flags <- c(lapply(which(abs(hd$rg_pct_diff) > TH), function(i) c(i, 4)),
           lapply(which(abs(hd$rm_pct_diff) > TH), function(i) c(i, 7)),
           lapply(which(df$ord == "NO"),           function(i) c(i, 8)))
style_cmp_table(df,
  groups = c(rep("Rolling vs. Greedy", 3), rep("Rolling vs. Myopic", 3), "Ranking holds"),
  subs   = c(SB, SA, paste0(DELTA, " pp"), SB, SA, paste0(DELTA, " pp"), "both runs"),
  bold_cells = flags,
  footer_text = c("% improvement = (rolling \u2212 comparison policy) as % of the comparison policy's value.",
                  paste0(DELTA, " pp = ", SA, " \u2212 ", SB, ", in percentage points; red = larger than ", TH, " pp.")))
```

I believe this is driven by different patterns in conversion risk: under GCAM, conversion to cropland is concentrated in the first two decades and then flattens to nearly zero mid-century and never recovers. This has two effects: the overall value of any acquisition policy through 2100 as compared to a do-nothing baseline is relatively low (since conversion risk in most decades is near zero), and the greedy/myopic policy significantly under perform the rolling policy in early decades (since they assumes continued high conversion risk when in fact conversion risk collapses). 

Under BAU, by contrast, the conversion risk is relatively stable across the entire study period. There is decadal variability, but there is no consistent mid-century collapse. This results in a reversal of the two effects: the overall value of any acquisition policy through 2100 as compared to a do-nothing baseline is higher; and greedy/myopic policy assumption of constant conversion risk is in fact pretty close to true.

I think this comparison is an interesting way to show how the model can help us understand the value of time-dependent acquisition policies in different systems. My primary take away from this is that the trajectory of conversion risk is more important than actual scale of conversion risk for determining the value/utility of a time-dependent acquisition policy as compared to a traditional (greedy/myopic) policy. I don't know that we need to report BAU results alongside GCAM results, but perhaps include the comparison as a sensitivity analysis in supplementary materials?

### 9/30/2026: Protected Area Removal

In examining the conversion risk, we realized that the previous
conversion risk included protected area in the total pool of potentially
available habitat, which artificially diluted the estimated conversion
risk. To address this, I overlayed the USGS Protected Area Database
(PADUS) and calculated the gross suitable habitat loss with protected
areas removed. This revised gross suitable habitat rate was used in the
risk of loss calculation (i.e., script 05); however, the other uses of
landcover data (such as distributing waterfowl density within a WMD)
continue to use the unmasked raster with protected areas included.

To overlay the PADUS layer, I used the PAD-US 4.1 Vector Analysis (USGS
GAP, 2024, PAD-US 4.1, https://doi.org/10.5066/P96WBCHS) and masked out
polygons marked as GAP Status Code 1-3 (which covers areas with
permanent protection, like National Parks, and areas where "low
intensity" land uses is allowed). I then created a 0/1 raster of
protected land within the PPR, and removed those areas when calculating
the gross habitat loss.

Updating the conversion risk to exclude protected areas increases the
comparative performance of the optimal model over the greedy model by
\~3-4 percentage points; it's noticeable, but not a fundamental change
to the takeaway message.

### 9/15/2026: Conversion Risk Update: Net vs Gross Habitat loss:

Delving in to the calculations of how I quantified conversion risk, I
realized that I was using net rather than gross habitat loss. This was
not conceptually consistent with what I presented, which I intended to
be the proportion of suitable habitat in time t that was lost by time
t+1 (a flow). Instead, I had calculated the difference between the stock
of suitable habitat in time t - t+1, which reflects both losses and
gains in suitable habitat.

I changed the calculations to see going from net to gross would affect
the estimate of conversion risk. I found that there is a fair amount of
habitat recovery in the FOREsce models, so some of those habitat gains
showed in the net calculation were concealing real habitat losses. The
table below compares the net vs gross habitat loss rate (gross \> net in
all decades but particularly mid-century). In addition, the use of the
net metric in the first model run meant that some EAUs had a "positive"
habitat loss (i.e., overall habitat gain), which I corrected for by
imposing a data-derived epsilon (floor). With the gross metric, that is
no longer needed (net loss \>= 0). The table also shows the percent of
EAUs that were "censored" by the artificial floor (i.e., which really
had habitat loss but which was hidden by habitat gain).

| Decade              | gross   | net     | \% of EAUs censored |     |
|---------------------|---------|---------|---------------------|-----|
| 2020–2040           | \~0.018 | \~0.017 | 0.5–7%              |     |
| **2050–2070 (4.5)** | \~0.002 | 0.0009  | **14–17%**          |     |
| **2050–2070 (8.5)** | \~0.002 | −0.0009 | **16–24%**          |     |
| 2080–2090           | \~0.003 | \~0.002 | \~4%                |     |

While we were missing meaningful habitat loss by using the net metric,
changing to the gross metric didn't substantially change the overall
model results. When I used gross instead of net habitat loss, this
increased the performance of the rolling model over the greedy model by
\~1-2 percentage points.

### 7/30/2026: Spatial Join error

I discovered an error in the spatial join of the extracted land cover
data and the model's data panel. I realized that the landcover data was
joined to EAUs by row position, which introduced errors- land
classification (% suitable habitat) was joined to the wrong EAUs.
Conversion risk (hazard) was the variable most affected- the trans_prob
were not attached to the correct spatial unit. Because duck density is
distributed according to % suitable, it also meant that duck
distributions were incorrect- but the scale of this error was mitigated
by the fact that WMD-scale determines the absolute amount of duck
density. This meant that WMD level abundance numbers are fine, but
distribution within WMD to EAUs was incorrect; cost numbers are
unaffected.

Because of this, I had incorrectly believed that most of the EAUs with
missing landcover data were concentrated in Winsom, which is why I
removed it- but I discovered that this wasn’t actually the case. There
were in fact multiple WMDs with at least a few EAUs missing data. I
needed to make a cut off threshold (% EAU with missing data above which
the WMD would be excluded); I decided to make a cap of 20% (i.e., any
WMD missing 20% of EAU land cover data would be excluded). This removed
one WMD (Fergus Falls), and left \~8 WMDs with some small % of landcover
data missing (2-13%). Note that this means that in those remaining WMDs,
the full WMD duck numbers are more densely concentrated in the remaining
EAUs.

When I fixed this, I saw that the spatial distribution of duck abundance
is now more clearly aligned with McKenna 2026 (good news!). Compare Fig.
1 with Fig. 1 from "results_07302026". There is also now a clearer
alignment of duck abundance and LOW acquisition cost: this is more
consistent with the literature, which regularly finds that the highest
duck abundance is in the western PPR where land prices are also lower.
But the major model findings don't change at all (i.e., rolling
outperforms both myopic and greedy, overall acquisition rate remains
low)

{{< pagebreak >}}

## 7/10/2026: Temporal alignment of benefit data

After the initial model run, I realized there was a problem with the
temporal alignment of the benefit data with the landcover data (and the
decision model itself). The benefit data is as follows:

- "Obs" = mean 2007–2017
- "3059" = mean 2030–2059
- "7099" = mean 2070–2099

Originally, I had aligned it as follows:

- "Obs" = mean 2007–2017 -\> 2020
- "3059" = mean 2030–2059 -\> 2050
- "7099" = mean 2070–2099 -\> 2100

After talking with Owen, I updated the alignment to use window midpoints

:   

- "Obs" = mean 2007–2017 -\> 2012
- "3059" = mean 2030–2059 -\> 2045
- "7099" = mean 2070–2099 -\> 2085

Notes: The 2020 baseline is produced by interpolating each RCP×GCM combo
on its 2012→2045 segment and then averaging across the four combos into
one shared period-0 row (preserves the shared-baseline used for the 2020
risk). Decades 2030/2040 interpolate on the 2012→2045 segment; 2050–2080
on the 2045→2085 segment; 2090 and 2100 are held constant at the 2085
value

I re-ran the model with this midpoint temporal alignment of benefit
data; saw little difference in model results. My takeaway is that we can
reasonably use this midpoint alignment, and importantly that it doesn’t
much matter for model results.

```{=latex}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}   % keep this whole table on one page
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-align-midpoint
```
